***Your behaviour is the raw material. Your prediction is the product.***

**Literal meaning:** **Surveillance capitalism** is **Shoshana Zuboff**'s term for the economic logic in which human behavioural data — generated by digital activities, devices, and platforms — is extracted, processed, and sold as prediction products to advertising and other markets. The raw material is human experience; the product is influence over future behaviour. Its key term is **behavioural surplus**: the part of the collected data that exceeds what a service needs to function, kept not to improve the product but because it has predictive value of its own. WhatsApp is an example: its messages are end-to-end encrypted, but the app still estimates where a user is from IP addresses and phone number area codes ([TechRadar, 2021](https://www.techradar.com/news/whatsapp-clarifies-policy-updates-is-it-too-late-already)).

**Origin:** **Zuboff** developed the concept over two decades, publishing the foundational academic paper in 2015 and the full argument in *The Age of Surveillance Capitalism* (2019). She identifies Google's 2000–2001 decision to use behavioural data from search queries to target advertising — initially as a side operation, then as the core business model — as the founding moment. The logic then spread to Facebook, the broader platform economy, and beyond, to insurance, finance, healthcare, and physical infrastructure. It also moved into the street: [["500 million people installed that app in 60 days."|Niantic's Pokémon GO (2016)]] turned millions of players into collectors of location data through the frame of a game, and in 2024 Niantic said that scans made by players were training a "Large Geospatial Model" of the physical world ([Maiberg, 2024](https://www.404media.co/pokemon-go-players-have-unwittingly-trained-ai-to-navigate-the-world/)).

> The economic logic in which human behavioural experience is claimed as raw material, processed into prediction products, and sold — named and analysed by **Shoshana Zuboff** in 2019.

**The Appeal:** **Surveillance capitalism** funds services that people value and use daily. The commercial logic is coherent: behavioural prediction is valuable to advertisers, and generating it funds the cost of platforms that users do not pay for directly. The trade — free services for behavioural data — produces real value for users. It is the same bargain as the [[Attention Economy]], paid in data instead of attention.

**The Friction:** **Zuboff**'s argument is that the trade is not disclosed, not negotiated, and not consensual in any meaningful sense. The system is built to keep the surplus invisible: "Our ignorance is their bliss," as she put it in a 2024 VPRO Tegenlicht interview. People who ask what happens to their data get reassurance instead of protection, which is [[Privacy Washing]]: Google kept recording users' movements after they had switched off Location History, according to a 2018 Associated Press report, and in 2022 settled with 40 US states for $391.5 million for misleading them ([Korn, 2022](https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/14/tech/google-location-tracking-settlement)).

The data does not stay where it was given. In January 2025 a hack of the location data company Gravy Analytics showed locations drawn from thousands of ordinary apps, Candy Crush, Tinder and MyFitnessPal among them, often without the app makers knowing; it is one of the largest [[Data Brokers]] and sells to commercial and government clients ([Cox, 2025](https://www.404media.co/candy-crush-tinder-myfitnesspal-see-the-thousands-of-apps-hijacked-to-spy-on-your-location/)). Government is a buyer, and it can become the next owner. In February 2025 Elon Musk's DOGE team, with engineers as young as nineteen, gained access to sensitive government databases and the Treasury's payment system ([Ingram, 2025](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/elon-musk-doge-usaid-treasury-government-rcna190450)), the merger of private infrastructure and public power that [[Muskism]] names. Two months later the acting director of ICE, Todd Lyons, said he wanted deportation to run [["Like Prime, but with human beings."|"like Prime, but with human beings"]] ([MacDonald-Evoy, 2025](https://azmirror.com/2025/04/08/ice-director-envisions-amazon-like-mass-deportation-system-prime-but-with-human-beings/)).

Leaving is harder than staying. Once photos, contacts and habits sit with one company, switching costs more than it is worth, which is [[Vendor Lock-in]], and a company that knows you will not leave can make the service worse: [[Enshittification]], Cory Doctorow's word for it. In 2024 Amazon put advertisements into Prime Video for people who already paid, and charged $2.99 a month to remove them ([Rizzo, 2023](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/09/22/amazon-prime-video-ads-start-in-2024.html)). Who pays is uneven: predictions built on data from an unequal past repeat that inequality at scale, as [[Algorithmic Violence]], harm done by automated systems that no one decided on. What makes it look normal is [[Dataism]], the belief that data is a neutral good, so that taking it is a neutral act. Van Iperen (2026) describes the result as environment design (*omgevingsontwerp*): people are not ordered, they are steered by the space that is built around them.

The newest collector is worn on the face. Meta's camera glasses, marketed through the [[Influencer]] Kylie Jenner, record the people around the wearer (Hoogenraad, 2026), and the Consumentenbond found that the recording light can be covered without the glasses noticing (De Zwaan, 2026). Two Swedish newspapers reported that wearers' private video goes to a contractor in Kenya to train the glasses' AI, where a worker described seeing *"everything, from living rooms to naked bodies"*: [[Ghost Work]], done on footage of people who never agreed to be filmed. When Roel Maalderink and Bits of Freedom made a satirical video about the glasses in September 2026, Meta removed it from Instagram as intimidating: [[Deplatforming]], by the maker of the product being criticised. The full story is in [[Biometric Surveillance]].

**Why This Matters:** **Surveillance capitalism** names the economic logic that underlies most of the Platform Mechanisms cluster. Once you see the logic — human experience as raw material — the specific mechanisms (**recommender systems**, **dark patterns**, dopamine loops) become legible as components of a single extractive system. The same logic also produces political power: [[Technofeudalism]], Yanis Varoufakis's term, describes platform owners who collect rent from users and businesses with no other option, and [[Broligarchy]] the network of tech owners who turned that commercial success into political influence. **Zuboff** compares the moment to the Gilded Age, when concentrated economic power was eventually reined in by law; the comparison gives hope, and it also sits uneasily with her claim that this power is unprecedented. The question then is not only how one person can opt out, but which rules would make opting out possible at all.
